screens.title: Introduction to AI in Games & State Machines
screens.subtitle: Why AI patterns matter and how FSMs give predictable, debuggable behavior

narration.text: In this lesson you will learn what game AI actually means in practice and why simple architectural patterns like finite state machines are indispensable. Game AI is not about creating thinking machines; it is about designing rules and decision systems that make non-player characters feel responsive, believable, and fun to interact with. You will see how categories such as pathfinding, perception, decision-making, and utility systems each solve a specific gameplay need. Then we will focus on the Finite State Machine pattern: a clear, single-state-at-a-time model that maps well to common enemy behaviors like waiting, patrolling, and chasing. I’ll give you concrete, implementable advice for designing transitions, keeping movement frame-rate independent, and avoiding common errors like null references or too many overlapping transitions. By the end of this chapter you should be able to design a basic FSM on paper, implement it in Unity using an enum and switch approach, and know when to reach for more complex architectures. Think of this as an essential toolkit: simple to reason about, easy to debug, and powerful enough for many game scenarios. What small enemy behavior will you build first?

keyIdea.title: Core Insight
keyIdea.text: Game AI is rule-based behavior design. FSMs offer a simple, testable pattern for agent behavior like Idle→Patrol→Chase.

Game AI focuses on patterns and systems that create believable, consistent NPC actions. screens.subtitle: Skills you'll develop in this chapter

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain the role of AI in games, choose appropriate AI types for gameplay needs, design a finite state machine, and implement a basic FSM in Unity. First, you will learn to articulate why AI is about behavior systems rather than consciousness, using examples such as pathfinding for navigation and perception for sensing the player. Second, you will differentiate categories like decision-making, utility systems, and perception and match each to a use case. Third, you will design an FSM on paper: identify states, entry and exit conditions, and safe transition rules. Finally, you will implement a working FSM in Unity using an enum and a state switch or methods for enter, execute, and exit, while avoiding common pitfalls like frame-rate dependent movement and null references. Each objective is a practical milestone you can verify by running a guard or enemy in a scene and observing stable transitions. As you work, ask whether a state is doing one responsibility and whether transitions are clear and testable.

narration.text: This second objectives slide emphasizes practical engineering habits: structuring state logic with entry, execute, and exit phases; writing clear transition conditions; and testing AI behavior using Unity tools like OnDrawGizmosSelected. You will practice guarding against null references, making movement frame-rate independent with Time. deltaTime, and keeping each state focused on one responsibility. screens.title: What is Game AI?
screens.subtitle: Understanding the purpose and categories of in-game intelligence

narration.text: Game AI is engineering: you build systems that let non-player characters behave in ways that matter to players. A clear definition is that game AI is the set of algorithms and rules enabling NPCs to navigate, perceive, decide, and act within the game world. For example, pathfinding algorithms let an enemy move around obstacles to reach a point, while perception code determines whether the player has been seen or heard. Decision-making decides whether to patrol, chase, or flee. Utility systems are another approach that rank possible actions by score and pick the best one. Each category answers a gameplay question: where to move, what to do, what to notice, and how to prioritize. A common misconception is that game AI must be complex; in reality simple rule-based systems often produce the most enjoyable and predictable gameplay. Consider a guard who patrols between two points and chases when the player is seen. That behavior can be implemented with a few conditions and an FSM, rather than a large learning model. The practical lesson is to separate concerns: put movement in one system, perception in another, and decision logic on top. That separation keeps your code testable and makes it easy to iterate on gameplay. Which gameplay question will you solve first?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Game AI = systems for navigation, sensing, decision, and prioritization to produce gameplay-focused behavior.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › What is Game AI?
What is Game AI?
A functional definition for game development
Game AI is about building rules and algorithms that turn simple inputs into meaningful, testable behavior. It groups into navigation, perception, decision-making, and utility systems. Think of these as separate tools you combine: a perception system tells the decision layer what it can sense, pathfinding tells movement how to reach a location, and decision logic chooses the next action.
Example: Guard
Patrol between points, detect player within range, then chase. Simple rules produce engaging behavior.
Misconception
More complexity does not equal better gameplay. Predictability and tuneability often matter more.
Key Takeaway

Treat AI as modular systems: perception, navigation, and decision layers make behaviors easier to build and test.

Categories
Pathfinding
Navigate around obstacles to reach targets.
Perception
Sense players using simple range and line-of-sight checks.
Decision
Rules or scoring systems that choose behavior.

screens.title: Types of Game AI — Practical Uses
screens.subtitle: Match AI categories to gameplay tasks

narration.text: Understanding the common types of game AI helps you choose the right tool for each gameplay problem. Start with pathfinding: it answers how an agent reaches a destination while avoiding obstacles. A concrete example is an enemy navigating around crates to chase a player. Decision-making is the layer that chooses actions. A simple finite state machine picks a single action per state, like Idle, Patrol, or Chase. Utility systems compare multiple potential actions and score them, which is helpful for varied or emergent behaviors, but can add complexity. Perception is separate: it produces sensory inputs, such as a boolean for whether the player is in range or a continuous noisy value for sound. Finally, consider priority or scheduler systems when multiple subsystems must coordinate, for example blocking movement while playing an attack animation. A common misconception is to conflate pathfinding with high-level decision; pathfinding only moves you from A to B, it doesn't decide why you move. Practically, keep perception and movement independent from state choice. When you design an enemy, explicitly ask: what do I sense, what do I want to achieve, and which system controls each part? This separation simplifies testing and tuning.

keyIdea.title: Match Tools to Tasks
keyIdea.text: Pathfinding moves, perception senses, decision logic chooses. Keep responsibilities separate for clarity.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Types of Game AI
Types of Game AI
Match each category to a concrete gameplay use
Pathfinding
Moves an agent from its current location to a target while avoiding obstacles. Example: an enemy uses a navigation mesh to reach the player.
Perception
Determines whether the player is seen or heard. Example: a ray or distance check triggers the Chase state.
Decision
Selects which behavior to run. Example: an FSM chooses idle, patrol, or chase based on timers and detection.
Utility
Scores multiple possible actions to pick the most desirable. Useful for varied NPCs but requires tuning.
Practical Tip

Keep perception and pathfinding separate from decision logic so you can test each system independently.

Quick Map
Use Pathfinding for movement
Use Perception to trigger states
Use Decision logic to choose action

screens.title: Finite State Machine (FSM)
screens.subtitle: Core properties and why FSMs are widely used

narration.text: A Finite State Machine is a formal model that defines a finite set of states and rules that govern transitions between them, with the guarantee that an agent is in exactly one state at any time. In games, that maps directly to behaviors such as Idle, Patrol, and Chase. The FSM's strengths are clarity and predictability: at any moment you can reason about what code runs because it is tied to the current state. A typical FSM supports entry logic, per-frame execution logic, and exit logic for each state. For example, entering Patrol might reset a waypoint index, executing Patrol moves toward the current waypoint, and exiting Patrol might stop movement or play a transition animation. A common misconception is that FSMs cannot express complex behavior. In fact, for many common enemy patterns a flat FSM is sufficient and very maintainable. If you need layered or nested behaviors, hierarchical FSMs add parent-child states to reuse logic without exploding the number of transitions. The practical test is whether you can draw the states and transitions on paper and explain every condition; if yes, an FSM is likely the right tool. How would you draw the transitions for an enemy that hides when health is low?

keyIdea.title: FSM Properties
keyIdea.text: An FSM is deterministic and single-state-at-a-time, making behavior easier to reason about and debug.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Finite State Machine
Finite State Machine (FSM)
Single-state clarity for predictable behavior
Key parts of an FSM include the list of states, the current state, transition rules, and optional entry and exit hooks for each state. When you implement in code, these translate to an enum of states and a state dispatcher that runs the logic for the active state each frame.
Entry
Setup values or play animations when a state starts.
Execute
Per-frame logic while in a state, such as movement or checks.
Exit
Cleanup or reset before a new state begins.
Key Takeaway

FSMs make behavior explicit: draw states and transitions, then implement each state's entry, execute, and exit to keep code readable.

Example FSM
States: Idle, Patrol, Chase
Transitions: Idle → Patrol after timer, Patrol → Chase on detection, Chase → Patrol when player lost.

screens.title: Designing a Simple FSM
screens.subtitle: Steps to identify states, transitions, and guards

narration.text: Designing an FSM starts with identifying the distinct behaviors your agent must show. Step one: list the states — for a guard, that might be Idle, Patrol, and Chase. Step two: for each state write the entry action, the execute action, and exit action. For example, entry into Patrol might set a waypoint index to zero; execute moves toward the waypoint; exit stops movement. Step three: define transition conditions and guards. A transition should have a clear, testable condition such as "player within detectionRange" or "idleTimer >= idleDuration." Step four: add buffers to avoid flicker — a small hysteresis on detection helps prevent immediate state bounce when the player skirts the edge of detection. Step five: iterate and trim states that duplicate responsibilities; if two states share large logic, consider merging or using a parent state in a hierarchical FSM. A common pitfall is adding too many micro-states for minor behavior changes; prefer clear, meaningful states. Finally, draw the diagram and walk through scenarios: what happens if the player disappears during Chase? You should be able to follow the transitions and explain recovery paths. That clarity is what makes FSMs effective in gameplay.

keyIdea.title: Design Steps
keyIdea.text: Identify states, define entry/execute/exit, write clear transition guards, and add buffers to prevent flicker.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Designing a Simple FSM
Designing a Simple FSM
Practical checklist for states and transitions
1. Enumerate meaningful states tied to gameplay goals — avoid micro-states for tiny visual changes.
2. For each state, write Enter, Execute, Exit logic so responsibilities are separate and testable.
3. Define clear transition guards, e.g. "playerDistance < detectionRange" or "timer >= idleDuration."
4. Add hysteresis or buffers to prevent rapid toggling between states when conditions hover at thresholds.
5. Draw scenarios to validate recovery paths and ensure no dead-end states.
Check Your Understanding

Can you explain what should happen if a player briefly flashes into range then leaves immediately? Add a buffer to the transition to avoid flicker.

Design Worksheet
State List
Idle, Patrol, Chase
Transition Guards
Idle → Patrol: timer; Patrol → Chase: detect player; Chase → Patrol: lost player > buffer

screens.title: Implementing an FSM in Unity (enum + switch)
screens.subtitle: A practical pattern using enums, switch, and state methods

narration.text: When implementing an FSM in Unity a straightforward and readable pattern uses a C# enum to represent states and a switch in Update to dispatch the current state's execute logic. The important engineering points are to cache references, guard against nulls, and multiply movement by Time. deltaTime. For example, an enum EnemyState { Idle, Patrol, Chase } neatly maps to a switch that calls IdleState, PatrolState, or ChaseState. Within IdleState you can increment a timer and call TransitionToState when the duration expires. PatrolState will move toward the current waypoint using Vector3. MoveTowards and update the waypoint index when close. ChaseState uses MoveTowards toward the player's position while checking for null and distance thresholds. Use TransitionToState to centralize exit and entry hooks; this helps when you later add animations or effects. A common mistake is directly modifying transform. position without Time. deltaTime, causing different speeds on different machines. Another mistake is checking for playerTransform == null only in ChaseState; perform global checks or caching in Start to avoid scattered null checks. This pattern is easy to read in the editor and quick to debug using logs and Gizmos.

keyIdea.title: Implementation Pattern
keyIdea.text: Use enums and a dispatching switch; centralize transitions and always handle nulls and delta-time for movement.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › FSM Implementation
FSM Implementation Pattern
Enums, switch dispatch, and centralized transitions
using UnityEngine;

public enum EnemyState { Idle, Patrol, Chase }

void Update()
{
    switch (currentState)
    {
        case EnemyState.Idle: IdleState(); break;
        case EnemyState.Patrol: PatrolState(); break;
        case EnemyState.Chase: ChaseState(); break;
    }
}
Important
Cache player transform in Start; check for null before using. Use Time.deltaTime for movement to remain frame-rate independent.
Transition function
Centralize state changes in TransitionToState to run exit and entry hooks consistently.
Common Mistake

Failing to multiply movement by Time.deltaTime causes inconsistent speed across machines.

Code Tips
TransitionToState
Reset timers and run entry logic when switching states.
OnDrawGizmosSelected
Visualize detection range and patrol points to debug behavior quickly.

screens.title: Idle, Patrol, and Chase — Behavior Details
screens.subtitle: Concrete logic, movement, and safety checks

narration.text: Let's break down the three example states — Idle, Patrol, and Chase — with concrete logic you can copy into Unity. Idle should be minimal: increment a timer each frame and transition to Patrol when idleDuration is reached. Always check for player detection in Idle so the agent can interrupt waiting. Patrol requires a patrolPoints array and a currentPatrolIndex. Use Vector3. MoveTowards to move toward the patrol target and check a small distance threshold to advance the index. Ensure you call transform. LookAt only when you want full rotation; projecting Y coordinates can avoid unwanted pitch or roll. Chase moves toward the player's position using chaseSpeed multiplied by Time. deltaTime. Importantly, guard against a null playerTransform: if it is null, transition back to Patrol to avoid errors. Also add a buffer when switching from Chase back to Patrol so the agent doesn't flicker when the player skirts the edge. A common debugging technique is to use OnDrawGizmosSelected to draw spheres for detectionRange and small spheres at each patrol point. That visual feedback makes it easy to tune distances and timers without stepping through code.

keyIdea.title: Behavior Breakdown
keyIdea.text: Idle uses timers, Patrol moves between points, Chase moves toward the player; always handle nulls and use delta-time.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Idle / Patrol / Chase
Idle, Patrol, and Chase
Concrete execution and safety checks
Idle
Increment idleTimer by Time.deltaTime. If idleTimer >= idleDuration then TransitionToState(Patrol). Also check detection each frame to allow interruption.
Patrol
If no patrol points, transition to Idle. Move toward patrolPoints[currentIndex] using Vector3.MoveTowards with patrolSpeed * Time.deltaTime. When within 0.1 units, advance index modulo length.
Chase
If playerTransform is null, TransitionToState(Patrol). Otherwise move toward playerTransform.position with chaseSpeed * Time.deltaTime and check distance to determine when to drop chase.
Pro Tip

Draw Gizmos for detection range and patrol points. Visual tuning beats blind trial-and-error.

Example Snippets
// Move with deltaTime
transform.position = Vector3.MoveTowards(transform.position, target.position, speed * Time.deltaTime);

// Distance check
if (Vector3.Distance(transform.position, target.position) < 0.1f) { /* reached */ }

screens.title: Enter / Execute / Exit Structure & HFSM
screens.subtitle: Organizing state code and when to use hierarchical FSMs

narration.text: A helpful architecture for state-based AI separates logic into three methods per state: Enter, Execute, and Exit. Enter runs once when the state begins and is ideal for resetting timers, triggering animations, or setting target indices. Execute runs every frame while the state is active and contains movement and detection checks. Exit handles cleanup, such as stopping effects or resetting flags. Centralizing transitions in one method, like TransitionToState, allows you to execute Exit on the old state and Enter on the new one consistently. When behaviors become large or you want reuse, consider a hierarchical finite state machine. An HFSM lets a parent state contain shared logic and child states handle specific variations. For example, a parent Combat state could include common targeting logic while child states implement Melee and Ranged behavior. The advantage is reduced duplication and clearer organization. A common misconception is that HFSMs are always superior; they add complexity and are only worth it when you have clear parent-child reuse. Start with a flat FSM, and refactor into HFSM only when duplication or complexity justifies it. The engineering goal is maintainability: fewer duplicated checks and clearer transition paths.

keyIdea.title: State Architecture
keyIdea.text: Use Enter/Execute/Exit for clarity. Move to HFSMs when parent-child reuse reduces duplication.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › State Architecture
Enter / Execute / Exit Structure
A pattern for readable state code
Enter()
Run once on state change to initialize timers, set animations, or prepare targets.
Execute()
Run every frame to perform movement, checks, and possibly call TransitionToState when conditions are met.
Exit()
Cleanup when leaving the state; stop sounds, reset flags, or cancel coroutines.
When to HFSM

Use a hierarchical FSM only when you see repeated logic that a parent state can provide without adding confusing depth.

HFSM Example
Parent: Combat
Shared targeting and attack timers.
Child: Melee / Ranged
Specific attack execution and ranges.

screens.title: Common Pitfalls and Misconceptions
screens.subtitle: What to avoid when building state-based AI

narration.text: When building state-based AI beginners often run into a handful of recurring pitfalls. First, adding too many micro-states turns the FSM into a hard-to-follow graph that increases bugs. If you catch yourself with dozens of nearly identical transitions, consider merging states or moving shared logic to a parent state. Second, forgetting to multiply movement by Time. deltaTime causes behavior that varies with frame rate, making testing unreliable across machines. Third, not guarding against null references for critical objects like playerTransform can lead to runtime exceptions; always validate and cache references in Start. Fourth, toggling states purely on immediate boolean checks without any hysteresis causes flicker when the player briefly enters and exits a detection boundary; add a small buffer to stabilize transitions. Finally, conflating pathfinding with decision logic complicates debugging: keep navigation, perception, and decision-making separate so you can test each in isolation. The remedy is intentional design: draw state diagrams, write clear transition guards, and test with Gizmos and logs. These habits are what turn prototypes into stable game systems. Common Pitfalls and Misconceptions means too many micro-states, missing delta-time, null refs, and no hysteresis are the most common causes of unstable ai.. In practical terms, what to avoid when building state-based ai. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Avoid These Mistakes
keyIdea.text: Too many micro-states, missing delta-time, null refs, and no hysteresis are the most common causes of unstable AI.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Common Pitfalls
Common Pitfalls & Misconceptions
Troubleshooting the usual problems
Micro-states
Too many similar states create maintenance overhead. Merge or use HFSMs for reuse.
Frame-rate dependent movement
Always multiply speeds by Time.deltaTime to ensure consistent movement across machines.
Null references
Cache and verify references like playerTransform in Start to avoid runtime errors.
No hysteresis
Add buffers to detection thresholds to prevent rapid state flipping.
Fix Pattern

Draw, test, and refactor: clear diagrams and editor Gizmos help you find and fix these issues fast.

Quick Checklist
  • Use Time.deltaTime on all movement
  • Cache transforms in Start
  • Draw Gizmos to validate ranges
  • Add buffers to detection thresholds

screens.title: Testing and Debugging AI in Unity
screens.subtitle: Using Gizmos, logs, and scene-driven checks

narration.text: Testing AI behavior in Unity is as much about visual feedback as it is about code correctness. OnDrawGizmosSelected is your friend: draw a wire sphere for detectionRange and small spheres at each patrol point so you can see exactly where transitions are expected to occur. Use Debug. Log selectively to announce state changes in the editor console, but avoid logging every frame which clutters output. Create a simple test scene with a player sphere you can move and a guard cube with patrol points; then step through scenarios: player enters detection, guard transitions to Chase, player leaves range, guard returns to Patrol. When behavior diverges from expectation, trace whether perception or decision logic failed. Is the detection condition incorrect, or is movement overshooting the target? Also test corner cases: what happens when patrolPoints array is empty or playerTransform gets destroyed? Add defensive code to handle those cases. Finally, validate frame-rate independence by testing at different target frame rates in the editor or by simulating lag; consistent movement proves your use of delta-time is correct. These tests help you iterate quickly and produce stable gameplay behavior.

keyIdea.title: Debugging Habits
keyIdea.text: Use Gizmos and focused logging, test edge cases, and validate behavior across frame rates for reliable AI.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Testing & Debugging
Testing & Debugging AI
Practical editor techniques to validate behavior
Gizmos
Draw detectionRange with a wire sphere and show patrol point markers so you can visually confirm where transitions occur.
Selective Logging
Log state transitions and important events, but avoid per-frame logs to keep the console useful.
Edge Case Testing
Test missing patrol points, destroyed player references, and rapid enter/exit scenarios to ensure graceful recovery.
Frame-rate Checks
Validate movement across frame rates to ensure Time.deltaTime is applied correctly.
Why it matters

Visual testing accelerates tuning and prevents surprises during playtests. It saves time compared to trial-and-error debugging.

Gizmo Example
void OnDrawGizmosSelected()
{
    Gizmos.color = Color.red;
    Gizmos.DrawWireSphere(transform.position, detectionRange);

    // Patrol points visualization
}

screens.title: Hands-on: Build GuardAI (Idle, Patrol, Alert)
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step lab to implement the GuardAI script and validate behavior

narration.text: This guided activity walks you through implementing the GuardAI script that demonstrates Idle, Patrol, and Alert behaviors. Start by creating a new C# script named GuardAI and define an enum GuardState { Idle, Patrol, Alert }. Expose public fields for playerTransform, patrolPoints array, detectionRange, patrolSpeed, alertSpeed, and idleDuration. In Start, try to find and cache the playerTransform using a Player tag as a fallback, and warn in the console if missing. In Update, use a switch on currentState to call HandleIdleState, HandlePatrolState, or HandleAlertState. Implement HandleIdleState to accumulate a stateTimer and transition to Patrol when the timer exceeds idleDuration; still check for player detection each frame so Alert can interrupt Idle. Implement HandlePatrolState to move between patrol points with Vector3. MoveTowards multiplied by patrolSpeed * Time. deltaTime, optionally briefly idling at each point. Implement HandleAlertState to move toward the player and transition back when the player leaves detectionRange with a buffer. Test in a simple scene: a cube for guard, a sphere for player, and empty GameObjects as patrol points. Use OnDrawGizmosSelected to visualize detectionRange. After testing, reflect on how clear transitions made debugging straightforward. What adjustment will you tune first — range, speed, or idle time?

keyIdea.title: Lab Objective
keyIdea.text: Implement GuardAI with an enum, state handlers, and editor-assignable patrol points; validate via scene testing and Gizmos.

narration.text: Here are three compact concepts to carry forward. First, treat game AI as modular systems: perception, navigation, and decision logic each have a distinct role. Keeping them separate improves testability and tuning. Second, a Finite State Machine keeps behavior predictable because the agent is in one clearly defined state at a time; implement states with Enter, Execute, and Exit to maintain clean control flow. Third, enforce engineering safety: cache references in Start, always multiply movement by Time. deltaTime, and use small buffers on transitions to avoid flicker. These three ideas — modularity, explicit state structure, and engineering safeguards — will help you design stable, maintainable AI for common gameplay scenarios. Key Concepts — Part 1 means modularize, structure states, and apply basic engineering checks for stable ai.. In practical terms, three essential ideas to retain. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Remember these ideas as you design AI

narration.text: Keep these three action reminders as you build: first, draw the FSM on paper before coding; that quick sketch prevents many logic errors. Second, prefer simple, testable rules that you can tweak in the editor instead of complex, opaque systems. For the guard example, tune detectionRange, idleDuration, and speeds via exposed inspector variables and test visually. Third, when behavior grows beyond a few states consider refactoring into a hierarchical FSM or switching to behavior trees if you need prioritized or reactive behavior at scale. But start simple; many enemies need only three or four states. Carry these reminders into your next prototype: sketch, expose parameters, test visually, and refactor when justified. In practical terms, three action-oriented reminders. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Action Reminders
keyIdea.text: Sketch before code, expose tunable parameters, and refactor to HFSMs or behavior trees only when needed.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Key Concepts
Action Reminders
Practical habits to apply immediately
Sketch First
Draw states and transitions before writing code to catch errors early.
Expose Tunables
Make detectionRange, speeds, and durations editable in the Inspector for quick iteration.
Refactor When Needed
Move to HFSMs or behavior trees only when duplication or complexity justifies it.
Final Thought

Start simple, test visually, and refactor intentionally. Those steps produce reliable gameplay faster.
